claim: The substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) is the primary output nucleus of the rodent basal ganglia.
source: The substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) is the primary output nucleus of the rodent basal ganglia (BG) and hence likely plays a key role in the behavioral functions, such as decision-making and action selection, suppression, or tuning, to which the BG contribute.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: SNr neurons receive GABAergic inputs from the striatum (direct pathway) and globus pallidus (GPe, indirect pathway).
source: SNr neurons receive GABAergic inputs from the striatum (direct pathway) and globus pallidus (GPe, indirect pathway).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about basal ganglia circuitry.

claim: SNr exhibits intrinsic spiking activity resulting in ongoing GABAergic outputs to specific thalamic sites.
source: The SNr exhibits intrinsic spiking activity, resulting in ongoing GABAergic outputs to specific thalamic sites, which are believed to suppress unwanted or spurious movements.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about SNr function.

claim: Indirect pathway GABAergic projections to SNr arise from the GPe, which engages in tonic spiking activity.
source: Indirect pathway GABAergic projections to SNr arise from the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe), which engages in tonic spiking activity; occur via basket-like synapses around the soma of SNr neurons; and exhibit short-term depression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Direct pathway inputs from striatum spike much more sparsely than GPe neurons.
source: Direct pathway inputs are delivered by striatal (Str) neurons, which spike much more sparsely; are located on distal dendrites; and exhibit short-term facilitation (Smith and Bolam, 1991; von Krosigk et al., 1992; Connelly et al., 2010; Lavian and Korngreen, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Striatal inputs to SNr are located on distal dendrites.
source: Direct pathway inputs are delivered by striatal (Str) neurons, which spike much more sparsely; are located on distal dendrites; and exhibit short-term facilitation (Smith and Bolam, 1991; von Krosigk et al., 1992; Connelly et al., 2010; Lavian and Korngreen, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Striatal inputs to SNr exhibit short-term facilitation.
source: Direct pathway inputs are delivered by striatal (Str) neurons, which spike much more sparsely; are located on distal dendrites; and exhibit short-term facilitation (Smith and Bolam, 1991; von Krosigk et al., 1992; Connelly et al., 2010; Lavian and Korngreen, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Earlier experiments showed excitatory effects along with inhibitory ones from stimulation of SNr-projecting Str neurons in vivo.
source: Moreover, earlier experiments showed excitatory effects along with inhibitory ones from stimulation of SNr-projecting Str neurons in vivo (Freeze et al., 2013), which could relate to chloride regulation as well.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: The model's dynamics matched a range of experimental findings on SNr firing patterns with inclusion of short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: We found that with the inclusion of short-term synaptic plasticity tuned to fit previous data, the model's dynamics matched a range of experimental findings on SNr firing patterns, including our own new results from optogenetic stimulation in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by comparison to experimental data.

claim: Variations in the level of GPe activity could interact with sparse SNr reciprocal interconnectivity to tune SNr synchrony.
source: Specifically, we predict that variations in the level of GPe activity could interact with sparse SNr reciprocal interconnectivity to provide an effective mechanism to tune SNr synchrony and the emergence of low-frequency oscillations, and we present experimental data based on optogenetic stimulation of GABAergic GPe terminals in the SNr that provides evidence of this effect.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model stated in the introduction.

claim: Variations in GPe activity can induce or suppress low-frequency oscillations in SNr.
source: Specifically, we predict that variations in the level of GPe activity could interact with sparse SNr reciprocal interconnectivity to provide an effective mechanism to tune SNr synchrony and the emergence of low-frequency oscillations, and we present experimental data based on optogenetic stimulation of GABAergic GPe terminals in the SNr that provides evidence of this effect.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claim: Ongoing high-frequency GPe activity could serve a modulatory role in action selection by adjusting the effectiveness of lower-frequency direct pathway Str signals.
source: We also predict that ongoing high-frequency GPe activity could serve a modulatory role in action selection by adjusting the effectiveness of lower-frequency direct pathway Str signals at pausing SNr outputs to downstream targets, as would be needed to allow action selection.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model stated in the introduction.

claim: The baseline firing rate of the SNr model is approximately 10 Hz.
source: The baseline firing rate (≈ 10 Hz) and action potential peak of the model are tuned to match experimental data from in vitro mouse and rat slice recordings (Richards et al., 1997; Atherton and Bevan, 2005; Yanovsky et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2011), while the AHP is tuned to match data presented in Higgs and Wilson, 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the model and supported by citations.

claim: The model's action potential peak is tuned to match experimental data from in vitro mouse and rat slice recordings.
source: The baseline firing rate (≈ 10 Hz) and action potential peak of the model are tuned to match experimental data from in vitro mouse and rat slice recordings (Richards et al., 1997; Atherton and Bevan, 2005; Yanovsky et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2011), while the AHP is tuned to match data presented in Higgs and Wilson, 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the model and supported by citations.

claim: The model's AHP is tuned to match data from Higgs and Wilson, 2016.
source: The baseline firing rate (≈ 10 Hz) and action potential peak of the model are tuned to match experimental data from in vitro mouse and rat slice recordings (Richards et al., 1997; Atherton and Bevan, 2005; Yanovsky et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2011), while the AHP is tuned to match data presented in Higgs and Wilson, 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the model and supported by citation.

claim: The magnitude of synaptic depression and facilitation of synapses onto SNr neurons was found to be largely independent of stimulation frequencies (10 Hz, 50 Hz, 100 Hz) in Connelly et al., 2010.
source: In Connelly et al., 2010, the magnitude of synaptic depression and facilitation of synapses onto SNr neurons was found to be largely independent of the tested stimulation frequencies (10 Hz, 50 Hz, 100 Hz).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: In the entopeduncular nucleus, short-term depression and facilitation are highly frequency-dependent according to Lavian and Korngreen, 2016.
source: In contrast, in a BG output nucleus analogous to the SNr, the entopeduncular nucleus (EP), a similar characterization of the short-term synaptic dynamics of GPe and Str projections found that short-term depression and facilitation are highly frequency-dependent (Lavian and Korngreen, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: The magnitude of synaptic facilitation of Str projections decreases in the EP for stimulation frequencies above 10 Hz.
source: Moreover, the magnitude of synaptic facilitation of Str projections was shown to decrease in the EP for simulation frequencies above 10 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to Lavian and Korngreen, 2016.

claim: Data in Connelly et al., 2010 was collected under voltage-clamp configuration.
source: A critical distinction between these studies is that data was collected under a voltage-clamp configuration in Connelly et al., 2010 and under a current-clamp configuration in Lavian and Korngreen, 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: Data in Lavian and Korngreen, 2016 was collected under current-clamp configuration.
source: A critical distinction between these studies is that data was collected under a voltage-clamp configuration in Connelly et al., 2010 and under a current-clamp configuration in Lavian and Korngreen, 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: The model was tuned to match voltage-clamp data from Connelly et al., 2010.
source: Based on these considerations, we tuned our model to match the voltage-clamp data from Connelly et al., 2010, as it is likely a better representation of the underlying short-term synaptic dynamics of GPe and Str inputs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: With tuning to voltage-clamp data, the model under current-clamp reproduces the synaptic dynamics reported in Lavian and Korngreen, 2016.
source: Interestingly, with this tuning, the short-term GPe and Str synaptic dynamics in our model when tested under current-clamp also reproduces the synaptic dynamics reported in Lavian and Korngreen, 2016.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 3.

claim: GPe synaptic depression and Str synaptic facilitation are strongly frequency dependent in the model under current-clamp.
source: Specifically, GPe synaptic depression and Str synaptic facilitation are strongly frequency dependent, and the magnitude of synaptic facilitation in Str synapses decreases for stimulation frequencies above 10 Hz (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 3.

claim: Short-term synaptic dynamics of inputs from GPe and Str in the EP are tuned in a similar way to those in the SNr.
source: Additionally, these findings suggest that short-term synaptic dynamics of inputs from GPe and Str in the EP are tuned in a similar way to those in the SNr.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Four distinct types of SNr firing rate responses were observed in simulations of somatic GABAergic projections from GPe: complete inhibition, no effect, excitation, and partial inhibition.
source: Four distinct types of SNr firing rate responses were observed: 'complete inhibition', 'no effect', 'excitation', and 'partial inhibition' (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 4.

claim: Two sub-types of partial inhibition occur in the model: deletion of one or a few spikes followed by a step reduction in firing rate, and complete inhibition followed by a late escape and continuation of spiking.
source: Additionally, two sub-types of partial inhibition occurred: (1) deletion of one or a few spikes followed by a step reduction in firing rate (Figure 4E1) and (2) complete inhibition followed by a late escape and continuation of spiking (Figure 4E2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 4.

claim: GPe synapses reach steady-state level of depression after approximately five stimulus pulses.
source: This lack of effect arises because these synapses reach steady-state level of depression after approximately five stimulus pulses, which occurs after just 125.0 ms when stimulating at 40 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation of the model behavior.

claim: Stimulation of dendritic GABAergic synapses resulted in the same four response types seen in the somatic compartment with an additional biphasic inhibitory-to-excitatory response.
source: Stimulation of the dendritic GABAergic synapses resulted in the same four response types seen in the somatic compartment with an additional 'biphasic inhibitory-to-excitatory' response and a slightly different pair of 'partial inhibition' responses (Figure 5B–F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 5.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of GPe and Str terminals in SNr resulted in a wide array of SNr response types.
source: In response to optogenetic stimulation, we found a wide array of SNr response types, which we classified into five categories: (1) complete inhibition - cessation of spiking; (2) partial inhibition - sufficient reduction of firing rate with or without a pause; (3) no effect - no change in firing rate; (4) excitation - sufficient increase in firing rate; and (5) biphasic - decrease or pause in spiking followed by an increase in firing rate above baseline.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: All response types could be induced by optogenetic stimulation of the GPe or the Str projection.
source: All response types could be induced by optogenetic stimulation of the GPe or the Str projection
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: The number of partially inhibited neurons with a 'long pause' increases with stimulation frequency for both GPe and Str stimulation.
source: Additionally, the number of partially inhibited neurons with a 'long pause' increases with stimulation frequency (GPe: 10 Hz, 1/25; 20 Hz, 8/26; 40 Hz, 13/29; 60 Hz, 16/24; Str: 10 Hz, 1/25; 20 Hz, 8/26; 40 Hz, 13/29; 60 Hz, 16/24).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents experimental data.

claim: Str projections are initially more effective at inhibiting SNr spiking relative to GPe projections (Str: 72.3–76.7% peak reduction, GPe: 43.1–61.9% peak reduction).
source: We found that Str projections are initially more effective at inhibiting SNr spiking relative to GPe projections (Str: 72.3–76.7% peak reduction, GPe: 43.1–61.9% peak reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: For both GPe and Str projections, the strength of inhibition decreases on average during the stimulation period.
source: Interestingly, for both GPe and Str projections, the strength of inhibition decreases on average during the stimulation period, consistent with slow accumulation of intracellular chloride.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 6.

claim: The loss of firing rate reduction was most prominent for Str stimulation at high frequency.
source: Moreover, the loss of firing rate reduction was most prominent for Str stimulation at high frequency, despite short-term synaptic facilitation known to occur at these synapses (Connelly et al., 2010; Lavian and Korngreen, 2016), consistent with the emergence of some excitatory and biphasic SNr responses in that regime.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 6 and citations.

claim: On average, a given SNr neuron receives GABAergic synaptic projections from 1 to 4 neighboring SNr neurons.
source: On average, a given SNr neuron receives GABAergic synaptic projections from 1 to 4 neighboring SNr neurons (Higgs and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation.

claim: The frequency of firing of the postsynaptic neuron repeatedly drifts below that of the presynaptic neuron at a rate of about 1 Hz.
source: Correspondingly, the distribution of presynaptic neuron phases when the postsynaptic neuron fires spreads out across the [0,1] interval and the frequency of firing of neuron the postsynaptic neuron repeatedly drifts below that of the presynaptic neuron, at a rate of about 1 Hz (Figure 8A5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 8.

claim: SNr neurons have been measured to spike at 10.4 ± 0.2 Hz and 10.7 ± 0.9 Hz under normal conditions in in vitro slice preparations.
source: Under normal conditions in in vitro slice preparations, SNr neurons have been measured to spike at 10.4 ± 0.2 Hz (Zhou et al., 2008) and 10.7 ± 0.9 Hz (Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The synchrony relationship between neurons is maintained regardless of the presynaptic neuron's firing rate.
source: These simulations show that the synchrony relationship between the neurons is maintained regardless of the presynaptic neuron's firing rate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 10.

claim: Slow oscillations have been reported in the SNr in vivo under dopamine depleted conditions in lightly anaesthetized and awake behaving animals.
source: Slow oscillations have been reported in the SNr in vivo under dopamine depleted (DD) conditions in lightly anaesthetized (Walters et al., 2007) and awake behaving animals (Whalen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Five oscillatory units with frequencies ranging from 1.46 Hz to 1.95 Hz (mean ± SD = 1.7 ± 0.204 Hz) were identified in SNr under DD conditions.
source: We identified five oscillatory units with frequencies ranging from 1.46 Hz to 1.95 Hz (mean ± SD = 1.7 ± 0.204 Hz, Figure 12C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 12.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of GPe terminals in the SNr had limited effect on SNr firing rates during a 30 s stimulation period.
source: In these units, optogenetic stimulation of GPe terminals in the SNr had limited effect on SNr firing rates during a 30 s stimulation period (Figure 12D; see Materials and methods for a full description of the experimental preparation and stimulation protocol).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 12.

claim: Stimulation of GPe terminals in the SNr significantly reduced the power in the PSD in the 0.25–4.0 Hz band.
source: Yet, stimulation of GPe terminals in the SNr significantly reduced the power in the PSD in the 0.25–4.0 Hz band (Figure 12E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 12.

claim: In tasks involving perceptual decision-making, visual motor responses (saccades) are thought to be triggered when evidence accumulates above some threshold level.
source: In tasks involving perceptual decision-making, visual motor responses (saccades) are thought to be triggered when evidence accumulates above some threshold level.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents established knowledge about decision-making.

claim: Experiments suggest that the BG is involved in regulating the dynamics of visual motor responses.
source: Experiments suggest that the BG is involved is regulating the dynamics of these visual motor responses (Basso and Wurtz, 2002; Basso et al., 2005; Shires et al., 2010; Sato and Hikosaka, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Evidence accumulation in the BG is thought to be represented by a ramping increase in the firing rate in striatal neurons of the direct pathway.
source: In the BG, evidence accumulation is thought to be represented by a ramping increase in the firing rate in striatal neurons of the direct pathway (Ding and Gold, 2010) that, above some threshold, generates a pause in SNr activity (Wei et al., 2015; Dunovan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: A pause in SNr spiking disinhibits downstream motor targets and allows the initiation of a selected action.
source: The pause in SNr spiking disinhibits downstream motor targets and allows the initiation of a selected action.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents established knowledge about basal ganglia function.

claim: Excitatory and biphasic GABAergic effects have been reported in other brain regions.
source: Excitatory and biphasic GABAergic effects are not unprecedented, however, as they have been reported in other brain regions (Haam et al., 2012; Astorga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Stimulation of striatal inputs to SNr in mouse brain slices at a slower rate of 2 Hz yielded consistent initial inhibitory effects rather than the diversity of SNr responses observed at higher frequencies.
source: In keeping with this idea, stimulation of striatal inputs to SNr in mouse brain slices at a slower rate of 2 Hz yielded consistent initial inhibitory effects rather than the diversity of SNr responses we observed (Simmons et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Previous in vivo experiments found that optogenetic stimulation of D1 Str neurons resulted in excitatory responses in 55% (15 of 27) of SNr neurons.
source: Consistent with this prediction, previous in vivo experiments (Freeze et al., 2013) found that optogenetic stimulation of D1 Str neurons resulted in excitatory responses in 55% (15 of 27) of SNr neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Given the sparsity of synaptic collaterals within SNr, unidirectional connectivity between SNr neurons would be the dominant motif observed.
source: In fact, given the sparsity of synaptic collaterals within SNr (Higgs and Wilson, 2016; Simmons et al., 2018), we expect that unidirectional connectivity between SNr neurons would be the dominant motif observed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference and supported by citations.

claim: The oscillations predicted by the model are slower than the β oscillations often discussed in the context of parkinsonism.
source: The oscillations that we predict will arise in SNr neurons are slower than the β oscillations often discussed in the context of parkinsonism.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison of model predictions to known phenomena.

claim: In mice, DA depletion increases SNr synchrony and promotes slow oscillations.
source: In mice, DA depletion increases SNr synchrony (Willard et al., 2019) and promotes slow oscillations (Whalen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: GABAergic inhibition in the SNr is attenuated by activation of D2 receptors.
source: This is consistent with previous a previous study which shows that GABAergic inhibition in the SNr is attenuated by activation of D2 receptors (Martin and Waszczak, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: DA depletion has been shown to accelerate saccadic perceptual decisions in humans.
source: Consistent with this idea, DA depletion has been shown to accelerate saccadic perceptual decisions in humans (van Stockum et al., 2011; van Stockum et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: GPe projections primarily form synapses around the soma but also form synapses on proximal dendrites.
source: GPe projections primarily form synapses around the soma but also form synapses on proximal dendrites (Smith and Bolam, 1991; von Krosigk et al., 1992), which we have ignored.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: SNr-projecting GPe neurons formed synapses with the soma and the distal dendrites of 54% and 32% of SNr neurons, respectively.
source: The study conducted by Smith and Bolam, 1991 found that SNr-projecting GPe neurons formed synapses with the soma and the distal dendrites of 54% and 32% of SNr neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The model assumes that GABAergic SNr collaterals form somatic as opposed to dendritic synapses.
source: Along similar lines, we assumed that GABAergic SNr collaterals form somatic as opposed to dendritic synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of a model assumption.

claim: The model does not include non-neuronal cells such as glia that can affect extracellular ion concentrations.
source: We also did not model non-neuronal cells such as glia that can affect extracellular ion concentrations, which could reduce the amplitude of the effects that we describe
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of a model limitation.

claim: The model does not include variability in extracellular concentrations of ions other than Cl− such as K+, which could affect SNr excitability.
source: the variability in extracellular concentrations of ions other than Cl− such as K+, which could affect SNr excitability
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of a model limitation.

claim: The model does not include slower components of synaptic depression that, if present, may yield a gradual weakening of inhibition over several seconds.
source: slower components of synaptic depression that, if present, may yield a gradual weakening of inhibition over several seconds
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of a model limitation.

claim: The model does not include direct effects of DA and other neuromodulators.
source: and direct effects of DA and other neuromodulators.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of a model limitation.
